claim: Climate change is accelerating plant developmental transitions coordinated with the seasons in temperate environments.
source: Climate change is accelerating plant developmental transitions coordinated with the seasons in temperate environments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about climate change effects.

claim: A cryptic function of flowering time control is to limit seed set of winter annuals to an ambient temperature window which coincides with a temperature-sensitive switch in seed dormancy state.
source: Modelling and field data reveal that a cryptic function of flowering time control is to limit seed set of winter annuals to an ambient temperature window which coincides with a temperature-sensitive switch in seed dormancy state.
evidence: This claim is supported by both modeling results and field data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The coincidence between seed set timing and dormancy switch is predicted to be conserved independent of climate at the expense of flowering date.
source: This coincidence is predicted to be conserved independent of climate at the expense of flowering date, suggesting that temperature control of flowering time has evolved to constrain seed set environment and therefore frequency of dormant and non-dormant seed states.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model simulations across different climates.

claim: Temperature control of flowering time has evolved to constrain seed set environment and therefore frequency of dormant and non-dormant seed states.
source: This coincidence is predicted to be conserved independent of climate at the expense of flowering date, suggesting that temperature control of flowering time has evolved to constrain seed set environment and therefore frequency of dormant and non-dormant seed states.
evidence: This is an evolutionary interpretation based on the modeling results.

claim: Late flowering can disrupt the bet-hedging germination strategy.
source: We show that late flowering can disrupt this bet-hedging germination strategy.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling of late flowering mutants.

claim: Life history modelling can reveal hidden fitness constraints and identify non-obvious selection pressures as emergent features.
source: Our analysis shows that life history modelling can reveal hidden fitness constraints and identify non-obvious selection pressures as emergent features.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Warmer temperatures are advancing plant phenology, with bud burst and flowering occurring earlier and the growing season becoming longer.
source: These show that warmer temperatures are advancing plant phenology, with bud burst and flowering occurring earlier and the growing season becoming longer (Menzel and Fabian, 1999; Fitter and Fitter, 2002; Cotton, 2003; Parmesan and Yohe, 2003; Cleland et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: For many species the flowering date is unaffected by climate change.
source: This is an adaptive plant response to shifting temperatures, because for many species the flowering date is unaffected by climate change (Fitter and Fitter, 2002), and plants that couple their phenology to temperature are more likely to have populations resilient to climate change (Willis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fitter and Fitter, 2002.

claim: Plants that couple their phenology to temperature are more likely to have populations resilient to climate change.
source: This is an adaptive plant response to shifting temperatures, because for many species the flowering date is unaffected by climate change (Fitter and Fitter, 2002), and plants that couple their phenology to temperature are more likely to have populations resilient to climate change (Willis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Willis et al., 2008.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana is widely distributed in the Northern hemisphere.
source: The model plant Arabidopsis thaliana is widely distributed in the Northern hemisphere and can be used to analyze phenology, including control by individual genes (Wilczek et al., 2009; Chiang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about Arabidopsis distribution.

claim: In northern Europe, Arabidopsis exhibits a primarily winter annual life history.
source: In northern Europe, Arabidopsis exhibits a primarily winter annual life history, but in central and southern Europe, summer rapid cycling and summer annuals appear alongside winter annuals (Thompson, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Thompson, 1994.

claim: In central and southern Europe, summer rapid cycling and summer annuals appear alongside winter annuals in Arabidopsis.
source: In northern Europe, Arabidopsis exhibits a primarily winter annual life history, but in central and southern Europe, summer rapid cycling and summer annuals appear alongside winter annuals (Thompson, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Thompson, 1994.

claim: A. thaliana is a ruderal species, primarily colonizing frequently disturbed habitats.
source: Importantly, A. thaliana is a ruderal species, primarily colonizing frequently disturbed habitats: the long-term persistence of such populations (and therefore fitness) is strongly dependent on seed behaviour and seed bank formation (Grime et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grime et al., 1981.

claim: The long-term persistence of A. thaliana populations is strongly dependent on seed behaviour and seed bank formation.
source: Importantly, A. thaliana is a ruderal species, primarily colonizing frequently disturbed habitats: the long-term persistence of such populations (and therefore fitness) is strongly dependent on seed behaviour and seed bank formation (Grime et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grime et al., 1981.

claim: Flowering time pathways have been elucidated genetically under laboratory conditions.
source: During the vegetative phase, plants have signalling pathways that couple progression to flowering to temperature and photoperiodic cues, and these pathways have been elucidated genetically under laboratory conditions (Andrés and Coupland, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Andrés and Coupland, 2012.

claim: Flowering time pathways are subject to positive selection in natural populations.
source: These same pathways are subject to positive selection in natural populations (Toomajian et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Toomajian et al., 2006.

claim: Late flowering Arabidopsis mutants delay reproduction by only a few days under field conditions.
source: However, when late flowering Arabidopsis mutants are analysed under field conditions they delay reproduction by only a few days, leaving the significance or their role unclear (Wilczek and et al., 2009; Chiang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wilczek et al., 2009 and Chiang et al., 2013.

claim: Temperature during seed set strongly influences life history by modulating seed dormancy after shedding.
source: Temperature during seed set also strongly influences life history by modulating seed dormancy after shedding (Fenner, 1991; Schmuths et al., 2006; Chiang et al., 2009; Kendall et al., 2011), but in contrast to the control of flowering time comparatively little attention has been paid to the role of this process in life history generation and adaptation.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is a simple linear relationship between temperature and the number of days from bolting to first seed set in Col-0.
source: We found a simple linear relationship between temperature and the number of days from bolting to first seed set, showing that seed set timing depended on ambient temperature.
evidence: This is demonstrated by laboratory experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Seed set timing depends on ambient temperature.
source: We found a simple linear relationship between temperature and the number of days from bolting to first seed set, showing that seed set timing depended on ambient temperature.
evidence: This is demonstrated by laboratory experiments.

claim: Seed set is much less dependent on photoperiod, with only photoperiods of 8 hr significantly delaying seed set.
source: Our data suggested that seed set was much less dependent on photoperiod, with only photoperiods of 8 hr significantly delaying seed set (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The thermal time model is a good predictor of seed set timing in the field (R2 = 0.43) for seed set in York in 2012 and 2013.
source: The model was a good predictor of seed set timing in the field (R2 = 0.43) for seed set in York in 2012 and 2013, and outperformed models that also included photoperiod components.
evidence: This is based on comparison of model predictions with field data.

claim: The thermal time model outperformed models that also included photoperiod components.
source: The model was a good predictor of seed set timing in the field (R2 = 0.43) for seed set in York in 2012 and 2013, and outperformed models that also included photoperiod components.
evidence: This is based on model comparison.

claim: Germination times from September to April lead to a very similar seed set time in late May at Gorsow, Poland.
source: Simulated at the most likely collection site, Gorsow, Poland, a key feature of the model is that germination times from September to April (winter and spring annuals) lead to a very similar seed set time in late May (Figure 1C), a behaviour caused in part by growth rate and flowering time control (Wilczek and et al., 2009) but further enhanced by the seed set responses to temperature.
evidence: This is shown by model simulation for Gorsow, Poland.

claim: Warmer climates advanced the seed set date, with 1°C rises in annual temperature giving about a 7-day advance in seed set time for winter annual cohorts.
source: Warmer climates advanced the seed set date, with 1°C rises in annual temperature giving about a 7-day advance in seed set time for winter annual cohorts from late June in Arkhangel'sk to early April in Valencia (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on model simulations across a climate transect.

claim: Winter annual seed set temperature was maintained at 14–15°C independent of latitude across sites with mean annual temperatures varying between 0.5°C and 17.5°C.
source: This behaviour has been widely observed in phenological studies, but our analysis also revealed a striking effect on temperature at first seed set: although mean annual temperature at the sites varied between 0.5°C and 17.5°C, winter annual seed set temperature was maintained at 14–15°C independent of latitude (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown by model simulations across the climate transect.

claim: The acceleration of flowering and seed set timing by warmer temperatures serves to stabilize the temperature range during which seed set begins.
source: Therefore, a key emergent feature of the model is that the acceleration of flowering and seed set timing by warmer temperatures serves to stabilize the temperature range during which seed set begins.
evidence: This is an emergent feature identified from the model simulations.

claim: Lower temperatures during seed production enhance seed dormancy in most angiosperm species.
source: Lower temperatures during seed production enhance seed dormancy in most angiosperm species (Fenner, 1991), but rarely has this response been characterized in detail.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fenner, 1991.

claim: Col-0 dormancy appeared related to the mean daily temperature and was not clearly influenced by daily temperature cycles.
source: Laboratory experiments revealed that Col-0 dormancy appeared related to the mean daily temperature and was not clearly influenced by daily temperature cycles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on laboratory experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At or below 14°C, Col-0 seeds produced are very dormant and do not germinate at high levels even after prolonged incubations under any temperatures.
source: Our results revealed a clear bi-phasic behaviour: At or below 14°C, seeds produced are very dormant and do not germinate at high levels even after prolonged incubations under any temperatures.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the germination experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Seeds set at 10°C are viable at harvest.
source: This is not due to low viability because seeds set at 10°C are viable at harvest (Kendall et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kendall et al., 2011.

claim: Above 14°C, high levels of germination were possible especially where seeds were incubated at similar or lower temperatures than experienced during seed set.
source: In contrast, above 14°C, high levels of germination were possible especially where seeds were incubated at similar or lower temperatures than experienced during seed set.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the germination experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: At temperatures above 14°C, seeds incubated in the dark experienced a transient period of primary dormancy loss during which time germination could occur if the seeds were given light, followed by secondary dormancy induction.
source: At these temperatures, seeds incubated in the dark experienced a transient period of primary dormancy loss during which time germination could occur if the seeds were given light, followed by secondary dormancy induction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the germination experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The high sensitivity of dormancy to a 1°C increase in seed maturation temperature supports the observation of a general increase in the temperature-sensitivity of gene expression in developing seeds relative to vegetative tissues.
source: This high sensitivity of dormancy to a 1°C increase in seed maturation temperature supports our previous observation of a general increase in the temperature-sensitivity of gene expression in developing seeds relative to vegetative tissues (Kendall et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kendall et al., 2011.

claim: A model with four parameters in which primary dormancy loss was dependent linearly on maturation temperature and secondary dormancy induction was dependent exponentially on imbibition temperature could be parameterised to provide a good fit to experimental data generated between 12 and 20°C (R2 = 0.84).
source: In fact, a model with four parameters in which primary dormancy loss was dependent linearly on maturation temperature and secondary dormancy induction was dependent exponentially on imbibition temperature could be parameterised to provide a good fit to experimental data generated between 12 and 20°C (R2 = 0.84; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and could match germination data in an experimental series set at 16°C and not used to train the model (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on model fitting to experimental data.

claim: The germination model could match germination data in an experimental series set at 16°C and not used to train the model.
source: In fact, a model with four parameters in which primary dormancy loss was dependent linearly on maturation temperature and secondary dormancy induction was dependent exponentially on imbibition temperature could be parameterised to provide a good fit to experimental data generated between 12 and 20°C (R2 = 0.84; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and could match germination data in an experimental series set at 16°C and not used to train the model (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on model validation with independent data.

claim: Behaviour of field-collected seed lots was qualitatively similar to that observed in the laboratory.
source: Behaviour of these lots was qualitatively similar to that observed in the laboratory.
evidence: This is based on comparison of field and laboratory germination data.

claim: The model-predicted temperature was close to the daily mean temperature in the last days before harvest for each seed batch.
source: In each case the model-predicted temperature was close to the daily mean temperature in the last days before harvest for each seed batch, as has been shown previously in barley (Gualano and Benech-Arnold, 2009).
evidence: This is based on comparison of model predictions with field temperature data.

claim: Mean temperatures below 14°C during seed set strongly inhibit germination.
source: The germination model predicts behaviour with two principle states obvious from the data: Firstly, mean temperatures below 14°C during seed set strongly inhibit germination.
evidence: This is a prediction from the germination model shown in Figure 3.

claim: Above 15°C the interaction between maturation temperature and imbibition temperature generally permits high germination rates.
source: Secondly, above 15°C the interaction between maturation temperature and imbibition temperature generally permits high germination rates.
evidence: This is a prediction from the germination model shown in Figure 3.

claim: Faster gain of secondary dormancy after imbibition at warmer temperatures is offset by the lower level of primary dormancy induced during seed maturation.
source: This is because faster gain of secondary dormancy after imbibition at warmer temperatures is offset by the lower level of primary dormancy induced during seed maturation.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the model behavior.

claim: Warmer climates have a longer summer window of high germination until at very warm locations the model predicts germination inhibition at the height of summer, due to fast secondary dormancy induction.
source: Warmer climates have a longer summer window of high germination until at very warm locations the model predicts germination inhibition at the height of summer, due to fast secondary dormancy induction.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The predicted transition from dormancy to germination takes place as the seed set temperature rises above 14°C, coinciding with the time of first seed set for winter annual cohorts, regardless of location.
source: Our models show that the predicted transition from dormancy to germination takes place as the seed set temperature rises above 14°C, coinciding with the time of first seed set for winter annual cohorts, regardless of location (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown by model simulations across different locations in Figure 3.

claim: Simulated Col-0 phenology generates a coincidence of seed set timing with germination physiology which is independent of climate over 25° of latitude.
source: Therefore, simulated Col-0 phenology generates a coincidence of seed set timing with germination physiology which is independent of climate over 25° of latitude, demonstrating that this aspect of Col-0 phenology is strongly buffered against variation in temperature.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model simulations across the climate transect.

claim: The model predicts that the low dormant progeny will enter a rapid cycle if the climate permits, flowering and setting seed later the same summer.
source: Our model predicts that the low dormant progeny will enter a rapid cycle if the climate permits, flowering and setting seed later the same summer (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model shown in Figure 3.

claim: The dormancy switch has the potential to control the proportion of seeds entering the seed bank and those that emerge immediately for a rapid cycle generation for production of further seeds.
source: This switch therefore has the potential to control the proportion of seeds entering the seed bank and those that emerge immediately for a rapid cycle generation for production of further seeds.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of the dormancy switch.

claim: GI confers a weak late flowering in field conditions of 7–10 days during summer.
source: GI confers a weak late flowering in field conditions of 7–10 days during summer while vin3-1 mutants generate a longer delay of 25–50 days (Sung and Amasino, 2004; Wilczek and et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: vin3-1 mutants generate a longer delay of 25–50 days in flowering.
source: GI confers a weak late flowering in field conditions of 7–10 days during summer while vin3-1 mutants generate a longer delay of 25–50 days (Sung and Amasino, 2004; Wilczek and et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both gi and vin3 mutants were predicted to set seed later in the year than wild type.
source: Both gi and vin3 mutants were predicted to set seed later in the year than wild type (Wilczek and et al., 2009), producing a greater proportion of seeds above the 14.5°C threshold and theoretically giving rise to more seeds capable of immediate germination.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: gi and vin3 mutants produce a greater proportion of seeds above the 14.5°C threshold and theoretically give rise to more seeds capable of immediate germination.
source: Both gi and vin3 mutants were predicted to set seed later in the year than wild type (Wilczek and et al., 2009), producing a greater proportion of seeds above the 14.5°C threshold and theoretically giving rise to more seeds capable of immediate germination.
evidence: This is an inference from the model predictions.

claim: gi mutations could double the number of low-dormant seeds in northern and central Europe but would have little effect at lower latitudes.
source: Assuming that seed set lasts for 1 month and follows a normal distribution, simulated across our transect the model predicts that gi mutations could double the number of low-dormant seeds in northern and central Europe but would have little effect at lower latitudes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a prediction from model simulations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mean temperature at shedding was raised from 14°C to 15°C for gi mutants at sensitive sites.
source: Mean temperature at shedding was raised from 14°C to 15°C for gi mutants at sensitive sites (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is shown by model simulations in Figure 4A,B.

claim: For vin3 the model predicts a rise in the mean temperature at maturation of almost 5°C, enough to commit most seeds to rapid cycling and severely curtail entry into the soil seed bank.
source: For vin3 the model predicts a rise in the mean temperature at maturation of almost 5°C, enough to commit most seeds to rapid cycling and severely curtail entry into the soil seed bank (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a prediction from model simulations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Small variations in flowering time may have dramatic effects on progeny life history in Arabidopsis by affecting seed dormancy.
source: Our analysis therefore suggests that small variations in flowering time may have dramatic effects on progeny life history in Arabidopsis by affecting seed dormancy, providing evidence for a previously unrecognized mechanism through which flowering time can affect plant fitness.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model analysis.

claim: Changing flowering time affects seed dormancy under field conditions more than flowering time itself.
source: This conclusion is supported by a recent study that shows that changing flowering time affects seed dormancy under field conditions more than flowering time itself (Chiang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chiang et al., 2013.

claim: Arabidopsis Col-0 can divide progeny into at least two distinct cohorts: obligate germinators which become summer rapid cyclers, and seeds which enter the soil seed bank even if initially exposed to light.
source: Our data and models show that in a striking coincidence winter annual seeds are set when the mean temperature is approximately 14–15°C, the temperature at which a major switch from the production of dormant to non-dormant seeds occurs. This inevitably divides progeny into at least two distinct cohorts: obligate germinators which become summer rapid cyclers, and seeds which enter the soil seed bank even if initially exposed to light (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the data and models, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: A similar transition has been observed in Capsella bursa-pastoris seeds: there is a transition in seed coat colour during seed set that alters dormancy and correlates with flowering time.
source: Notably, a similar transition has been observed in Capsella bursa-pastoris seeds: in this case there is a transition in seed coat colour during seed set that alters dormancy and correlates with flowering time (Toorop et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Toorop et al., 2012.

claim: In Arabidopsis seed coat, pigmentation is affected by the temperature during seed set.
source: In Arabidopsis seed coat, pigmentation is affected by the temperature during seed set (MacGregor et al., 2015), again demonstrating control by the mother plant.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to MacGregor et al., 2015.

claim: Similar bet-hedging germination strategies have been described frequently across flowering plants.
source: Similar bet-hedging germination strategies have been described frequently across flowering plants suggesting wide general relevance (Childs et al., 2010), but further studies are required to understand whether this is a common strategy for Arabidopsis in locations where temperatures are warm enough to permit life history variation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Childs et al., 2010.

claim: Control of progeny behaviour likely generates a major selection pressure on flowering time control because seed bank loading is a key component of fitness in ruderal plant populations.
source: Because seed bank loading is a key component of fitness in ruderal plant populations (Grime, 1988), control of progeny behaviour likely generates a major selection pressure on flowering time control.
evidence: This is an inference based on the importance of seed bank loading, supported by a citation to Grime, 1988.

claim: In Norway the mean lifespan of Arabidopsis in the seed bank was estimated at between 1 and 8 years.
source: Genetic analyses of Arabidopsis fitness have frequently considered yield to be paramount, but seed behaviour and seed bank dynamics are central to long-term population persistence: in Norway the mean lifespan of Arabidopsis in the seed bank was estimated at between 1 and 8 years (Lundemo et al., 2009), but work to understand genetic contributions to seed bank dynamics is in its infancy.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lundemo et al., 2009.

claim: Col-0 germination in autumn or spring gives a similar flowering date in May.
source: Col-0 germination in autumn or spring gives a similar flowering date in May.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the model simulations.

claim: Col-0 can operate equally well as a summer or winter annual.
source: This suggests that Col-0 can operate equally well as a summer or winter annual.
evidence: This is an inference from the model behavior.

claim: Seed set in the laboratory at 15°C or seed set in the field conditions germinate in the soil in both autumn and spring emergence windows.
source: This prediction is supported by field emergence data, which shows that seed set in the laboratory at 15°C or seed set in the field conditions germinate in the soil in both autumn and spring emergence windows (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by field emergence data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Seeds of the Cape Verde Island accession germinate only in an autumn emergence window in central England.
source: Previously it has been shown that seeds of the Cape Verde Island accession germinate only in an autumn emergence window in central England (Footitt et al., 2011), whereas accession Bur-0 shows only a spring emergence window (Footitt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Footitt et al., 2011.

claim: Accession Bur-0 shows only a spring emergence window.
source: Previously it has been shown that seeds of the Cape Verde Island accession germinate only in an autumn emergence window in central England (Footitt et al., 2011), whereas accession Bur-0 shows only a spring emergence window (Footitt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Footitt et al., 2013.

claim: Winter and spring annual behaviour does not necessarily require different genotypes and are not mutually exclusive strategies.
source: However, our work shows that winter and spring annual behaviour does not necessarily require different genotypes and are not mutually exclusive strategies.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of Col-0 behavior.

claim: Both spring and autumn germination windows have been described in coastal but not montane Spanish populations.
source: Both spring and autumn germination windows have also been described in coastal but not montane Spanish populations (Montesinos et al., 2009), suggesting that the strategy employed by Col-0 is of wide relevance in some ecological contexts.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Montesinos et al., 2009.

claim: Col-0 winter annual behaviour requires a strong slowing of growth rates under low temperatures.
source: In the case of Col-0, winter annual behaviour appears to require (1) a strong slowing of growth rates under low temperatures, showing that growth rate can be as important as leaf number in determining timing of the floral transition in natural populations, and (2) strong tendency towards fast secondary dormancy induction combined with an autumn germination window.
evidence: This is an inference about the requirements for winter annual behavior in Col-0.

claim: Growth rate can be as important as leaf number in determining timing of the floral transition in natural populations.
source: In the case of Col-0, winter annual behaviour appears to require (1) a strong slowing of growth rates under low temperatures, showing that growth rate can be as important as leaf number in determining timing of the floral transition in natural populations, and (2) strong tendency towards fast secondary dormancy induction combined with an autumn germination window.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of Col-0 behavior.

claim: Col-0 winter annual behaviour requires strong tendency towards fast secondary dormancy induction combined with an autumn germination window.
source: In the case of Col-0, winter annual behaviour appears to require (1) a strong slowing of growth rates under low temperatures, showing that growth rate can be as important as leaf number in determining timing of the floral transition in natural populations, and (2) strong tendency towards fast secondary dormancy induction combined with an autumn germination window.
evidence: This is an inference about the requirements for winter annual behavior in Col-0.

claim: Strong FRI and FLC alleles and other late flowering alleles confer flowering delays primarily on summer germinants.
source: In contrast, strong FRI and FLC alleles and other late flowering alleles also confer flowering delays primarily on summer germinants (Wilczek and et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wilczek et al., 2009.

claim: The increased prevalence of strong FLC alleles at northern latitudes is good evidence that an advantage of this strategy is maximisation of energy capture in short growing seasons through early seedling establishment.
source: The increased prevalence of strong FLC alleles at northern latitudes (Shindo et al., 2006; Li et al., 2014) is good evidence that an advantage of this latter strategy is maximisation of energy capture in short growing seasons through early seedling establishment, rather than generation of winter annual behaviour itself.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Shindo et al., 2006 and Li et al., 2014.

claim: At mid-latitudes stronger FRI/FLC alleles have the potential to push back seed set of summer germinants into autumn.
source: At mid-latutides stronger FRI/FLC alleles have the potential to push back seed set of summer germinants into autumn (Wilczek and et al., 2009), and during autumn the temperature again passes back through the critical 14–15°C range.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wilczek et al., 2009.

claim: During autumn the temperature passes back through the critical 14–15°C range.
source: At mid-latutides stronger FRI/FLC alleles have the potential to push back seed set of summer germinants into autumn (Wilczek and et al., 2009), and during autumn the temperature again passes back through the critical 14–15°C range.
evidence: This is an observation about temperature patterns.

claim: Latitudinal clines in seed dormancy have been described, whereby accessions from more northerly latitudes exhibit lower primary dormancy levels.
source: In addition to flowering time, latitudinal clines in seed dormancy have also been described, whereby accessions form more northerly latitudes exhibit lower primary dormancy levels (Atwell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Atwell et al., 2010.

claim: Decreasing temperature during seed maturation strongly increases primary dormancy.
source: Given that decreasing temperature during seed maturation strongly increases primary dormancy, our analysis suggests that these opposing genetic and environmental trends could offset each other in field conditions allowing maintenance of progeny behavioural strategies.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data and model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Opposing genetic and environmental trends in dormancy could offset each other in field conditions allowing maintenance of progeny behavioural strategies.
source: Given that decreasing temperature during seed maturation strongly increases primary dormancy, our analysis suggests that these opposing genetic and environmental trends could offset each other in field conditions allowing maintenance of progeny behavioural strategies.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis.

claim: Variation at the DELAY OF GERMINATION1 (DOG1) locus is a major determinant of natural variation in primary seed dormancy.
source: Variation at the DELAY OF GERMINATION1 (DOG1) locus is a major determinant of natural variation in primary seed dormancy (Bentsink et al., 2006; Chiang et al., 2011) and temperature-regulation of DOG1 transcript levels during seed maturation (Chiang et al., 2011; Kendall et al., 2011; Chiang et al., 2013) may therefore play an important role in adaptation of seed dormancy to changing temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bentsink et al., 2006 and Chiang et al., 2011.

claim: Temperature-regulation of DOG1 transcript levels during seed maturation may play an important role in adaptation of seed dormancy to changing temperatures.
source: Variation at the DELAY OF GERMINATION1 (DOG1) locus is a major determinant of natural variation in primary seed dormancy (Bentsink et al., 2006; Chiang et al., 2011) and temperature-regulation of DOG1 transcript levels during seed maturation (Chiang et al., 2011; Kendall et al., 2011; Chiang et al., 2013) may therefore play an important role in adaptation of seed dormancy to changing temperatures.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Chiang et al., 2011; Kendall et al., 2011; Chiang et al., 2013.

claim: It is possible to model Arabidopsis populations over several generations using thermal time models.
source: Recent articles also show that it is possible to model Arabidopsis populations over several generations using thermal time models (Donohue et al., 2014; Burghardt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Donohue et al., 2014 and Burghardt et al., 2015.

claim: Multi-generation models can recreate aspects of Arabidopsis phenology observed previously under field conditions at different latitudes, including the ability of Col-0 to adopt winter annual, summer annual, and rapid cycling life histories.
source: The process reveals theoretical interactions between primary dormancy and flowering time that can recreate aspects of Arabidopsis phenology observed previously under field conditions at different latitudes, including the ability of Col-0 to adopt winter annual, summer annual, and rapid cycling life histories described here.
evidence: This is based on the multi-generation modeling studies cited.

claim: Germination behaviour such as temperature regulation of primary dormancy depth and secondary dormancy kinetics are necessary to understand life history control.
source: Our analysis also shows that germination behaviour not included in these models such as temperature regulation of primary dormancy depth and secondary dormancy kinetics are necessary to understand life history control.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The bet-hedging strategy is stable over latitude throughout Europe, except in the far north where temperature is too cool to generate germinating cohorts.
source: A further feature of Col-0 phenology is that the bet-hedging strategy is stable over latitude throughout Europe, except in the far north where temperature is too cool to generate germinating cohorts.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model simulations across the climate transect.

claim: The bet-hedging strategy is stable in respect to simulated warming, except in respect to time of year of seed set.
source: It is also stable in respect to simulated warming (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), except in respect to time of year of seed set.
evidence: This is shown by model simulations in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lack of local adaptation in the bet-hedging strategy could facilitate population stability in changing environments or enable rapid colonization of new territories.
source: This surprising lack of local adaptation could facilitate population stability in changing environments or enable rapid colonization of new territories, if timing of seed set was under no further constraints.
evidence: This is a speculation about the implications of the model results.

claim: Integration of life history modelling with behaviour of genetic variants has the potential to reveal fitness tradeoffs across the whole life history and identify non-obvious selection pressures as emergent features.
source: Our work suggests that integration of life history modelling with behaviour of genetic variants has the potential to reveal fitness tradeoffs across the whole life history and identify non-obvious selection pressures as emergent features.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about the utility of the modeling approach.

claim: The thermal time model from bolting to first seed set was constructed using laboratory experiments at various constant temperatures.
source: Laboratory experiments from bolting to first seed set at various constant temperatures used to constrain the seed set thermal time model.
evidence: This is described in the methods and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The seed set model was tested using nine growings of plants in field trials.
source: Field trial testing of the seed set model using nine growings of a minimum of five plants showing mean and standard error of bolting date and time to seed set.

claim: Col-0 is known to originate from central Europe.
source: The precise location for the collection of Col-0 is uncertain but it is known to originate from central Europe (Robbelen, 1965; C Dean Personal communication).

claim: The photothermal model did not outperform the simple thermal time model for predicting seed set timing.
source: The photothermal model (R2 = 0.28) did not outperform the simple thermal time model (R2 = 0.42): therefore, we elected to use a simple thermal time model of Arabidopsis seed set (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of model performance.

claim: Germination is possible in the absence of dormancy.
source: To allow simulation of the whole life history, we developed a predictive framework for Col-0 germination probability and constructed a germination model based on the following assumptions used previously for similar studies (Totterdell and Roberts, 1979; Bradford, 2005; Batlla et al., 2009): (1) germination is possible in the absence of dormancy
evidence: This is an assumption of the germination model, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Primary dormancy depth is fixed at harvest and is lost during imbibition.

evidence: This is an assumption of the germination model, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The onset of secondary dormancy begins independently during seed imbibition.
source: (3) the onset of secondary dormancy (dormancy induced de novo after imbibition) begins independently during seed imbibition.
evidence: This is an assumption of the germination model, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Secondary dormancy appeared to be induced faster at warmer imbibition temperatures.
source: We noted that secondary dormancy appeared to be induced faster at warmer imbibition temperatures (Figure 2), and fixing this relationship in the model revealed that close matches to experimental data could be produced if initial primary dormancy was modelled as a function of the temperature during seed maturation (see 'Materials and methods' and Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The model-predicted temperature for field-grown seed was close to the daily mean temperature in the last days before harvest for each seed batch, as has been shown previously in barley.
source: In each case the model-predicted temperature was close to the daily mean temperature in the last days before harvest for each seed batch, as has been shown previously in barley (Gualano and Benech-Arnold, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with field data and a citation to Gualano and Benech-Arnold, 2009.
